title: Matthew 23:13–15
context: After exposing honor-seeking religion, Jesus opens the seven woes. The first strike hypocrisy that blocks the kingdom and mission that multiplies ruin. (ESV omits v. 14, present in some manuscripts as a widows’-houses woe.)

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on Jesus opens the seven woes—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Matthew 23:13–15.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Wo unto you, scribes - I think the fourteenth and thirteenth verses should be transposed. This transposition is authorized by some of the best MSS., versions, and fathers. The fourteenth is wanting in the BDL., and in many others of inferior note, as well as in several of the versions.
arminian.source: Commentary on the New Testament (on Matt 23:13–15)

reformed.quote: Christ pronounces a curse on them, because they pervert their office to the general destruction of the whole people; for since the government of the Church was in their hands, they ought to have been, as it were, porters for the kingdom of heaven. What purpose is served by religion and holy doctrine but to open heaven to us?
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 23:13–15)

verses.text: "But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces. For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in.
verses.arminianNotes:
Woe names grief and judgment. They shut the kingdom in people’s faces—neither entering nor letting others enter who would.

Classical Arminians hear a tragic abuse of influence: grace’s door is blocked by false teaching and example. Those who “would enter” show real inclination met with obstruction; leaders bear heavy guilt for hindering sincere seekers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Woe from the King exposes hypocrites who shut heaven’s kingdom. They refuse entry and obstruct others.

Reformed gravity: Christ alone opens and shuts with ultimate authority. False shepherds oppose His kingdom; their barrier is real sin under His judicial word, and the woe is not empty rhetoric.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat the shutting of the kingdom as culpable hypocrisy. Arminians typically emphasize blocked seekers who truly would enter; Reformed readers typically emphasize Christ’s judicial woe against leaders who oppose His kingdom under God’s righteous verdict.

verses.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zealous mission without truth: sea and land for one convert, then a disciple twice a child of hell. Evangelistic energy can deepen ruin when the gospel is twisted.

Arminian pastoral warning: grace cares about converts’ destiny. Mission must lead people to Christ, not into a harder hypocrisy. The woe summons repentance for teachers and converts alike.
verses.reformedNotes:
Proselytizing zeal ends in doubled Gehenna-children. Activity is not faithfulness.

Reformed sobriety: God weighs mission by its fruit under truth. False religion reproduces itself; Christ’s woe judges both the makers and the system that multiplies heirs of wrath.
